30 Days of Vibe Coding | Day 27: Pull Requests and Automatic Code Review with CodeRabbit

Yesterday we did a quick review: we moved the "budget alerts" feature off the original "Out" list, made a plan with Plan Mode, built it, and finally pushed to main so GitHub Actions deployed it automatically.
But next I want to talk about a more proper development workflow: the PR (Pull Request) workflow.
In short, before our code lands on main and gets deployed, the changes go through a few checks first so we don't break the live site. And the whole thing is automatic.
Back on Day 25 I briefly mentioned branches. I said you didn't need to understand them yet, but now it's time to actually spend a bit of time on them.
First off, in a proper development workflow, we keep production and development separate:
This is the main branch. Every push to it deploys automatically to the live URL, which is the public-facing environment. So once something's out there, real users are seeing it.
This is the develop branch. It doesn't deploy to the live URL. It's mainly where developers test, check their work, and fix bugs.

A copy, or draft, split off from main or develop. You can make changes on this draft, test them, and check them without affecting main or develop. Common ones are feature branches, bugfix branches, hotfix branches, and so on.

So starting today, the expense tracker app follows this flow too. Every time we change anything, we branch off develop, merge back into develop when we're done, test it in the test environment, and once everything checks out, merge develop into main to go live.

Basically, think of it as a request form. It says: "I'd like to merge this draft (the feature branch) into develop" (or "merge develop into main"). And that request form can come with a few checks, like:
Automated tests: did this change break anything that used to work?
AI review: does this change have any security concerns or code quality problems?
Human review: does this change follow the team's conventions, and is the code style okay?
That's the process we're adding here. Once it's in place, the whole thing looks like this:

With the basics down, we're going to bring in an AI code review service called CodeRabbit, so every PR gets reviewed automatically the moment it opens, with comments left in Chinese (or whatever language you set).

I keep mentioning? In short, it's an AI code review service. Once you install it on your GitHub repository, whenever certain PRs get opened, CodeRabbit automatically reviews the changes and leaves comments right on the PR.
So... an AI code review service can't be completely free, right? After all, we've said over and over that the most expensive part of AI is compute.
And you'd be right. CodeRabbit has paid plans, billed monthly per developer. The Essentials plan is $30 per person per month ($24 if you pay annually).

But it's really generous with public repositories. If your repo is public, you can use PR code review for free once it's installed, no credit card needed. On the other hand, for a private repo the free plan only gives you PR summaries. The real line-by-line review is paid.
project is public, so we can demo it right away.

A lot of services build their free plans around open source projects, because open source gives back to the community. That's part of why we went with a public repository for this project.
The users these companies actually make money from are private repositories on paid plans, since those are usually for commercial use. That's where the value is for them, and those users are more willing to pay.
So why do we still need CodeRabbit when we already set up code-reviewer back on Day 19?

Because code-reviewer only does anything when you call it, while CodeRabbit lives on GitHub and runs automatically whenever you open a PR. Put that together with the Hooks and CLAUDE.md we learned earlier, and the full development flow ends up looking like this:

Have the AI add the config
What's next? Let's try opening a PR and see whether CodeRabbit reviews it automatically.
Before that, though, there's some setup to do: adding a config file called .coderabbit.yaml to the project. This file mainly sets CodeRabbit's review language, which branches to review, and so on.
Same as always, just hand it to the AI. Type
to clear the conversation, then enter this prompt:

I want to add a PR workflow to this project. main is production and develop is development. Please do four things:

1. Add .github/workflows/test.yml so that whenever there's a PR to merge into develop or main, it automatically runs npm ci, npm test, and npm run build.
2. Add .coderabbit.yaml, set the review language to zh-TW, and make PRs that merge into develop get reviewed automatically too.
3. Add rules to CLAUDE.md: from now on, every change branches off develop, pushes the branch, and opens a PR to merge back into develop; when it's time to go live, open a develop → main PR; never push directly to develop or main.
4. When all of that is done, commit and push to main. This is the last direct push. Then create a develop branch from main and push it.

What do you do with CodeRabbit's comments?
The tests are covered. So what about all those comments CodeRabbit left?

Here's the big-picture rule: CodeRabbit labels its suggestions high, medium, or low. Focus mainly on high and medium. For the low ones, talk them over with the AI and see whether they really need fixing.
Because sometimes AI is a little too sensitive. Say you've got a
in your code. CodeRabbit might suggest removing it, but maybe that
is something you need while testing. In that case you can just ignore it.
So how do you get the AI to fix CodeRabbit's suggestions? A couple of ways:
Manually copy the CodeRabbit comment, paste it to the AI, and ask it to fix it.
Have the AI go read CodeRabbit's comments directly, which you'll need the Claude in Chrome extension for.
Personally, I use the second one more often.
That's about it for this one, so let's sum up:

Keep production (main) and development (develop) separate. Every change branches off develop, merges back into develop first, and only after you've confirmed it's fine does develop get merged into main to go live.
A PR is a request form. Before any change gets into develop or main, it has to pass checks like automated tests and AI review.
CodeRabbit is free for public repositories, and because it lives on GitHub, it reviews automatically whenever you open a PR. Unlike code-reviewer, you don't have to remember to call it.
Besides CodeRabbit, you can also add Copilot under Reviewers on a GitHub PR, so one more AI looks over your code.
You don't have to fix every one of CodeRabbit's suggestions. Focus on the high and medium ones, and talk the low ones over with the AI to see whether they really need fixing.
And don't forget the homework: make Actions go red once with your own hands.
